title: SQL Transactions & Isolation Levels: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense study series on how relational databases keep concurrent work correct: ACID guarantees, the read anomalies each isolation level permits, the locking and MVCC machinery underneath, deadlocks, and the practical trade-offs of picking a level in Postgres, MySQL, and SQL Server.

chapters.title: What a Transaction Actually Is
points: Definition: a transaction is a unit of work that moves the database from one consistent state to another, all-or-nothing
Transaction boundaries: BEGIN / START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT | ROLLBACK, and autocommit mode where every statement is its own transaction
The canonical example: transferring 100 from account A to account B is two UPDATEs that must both apply or neither
Implicit vs explicit transactions: MySQL and Postgres autocommit by default; SQL Server needs SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS ON or explicit BEGIN TRAN
SAVEPOINT sp1 / ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1 / RELEASE SAVEPOINT for partial rollback inside a longer transaction
DDL and transactions: Postgres can roll back CREATE TABLE; MySQL and Oracle implicitly commit on DDL, so a mid-transaction ALTER silently ends your transaction
Transaction states: active, partially committed, committed, failed, aborted
Read-only transactions (SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY) and why they let the engine skip work
A rolled-back transaction still consumes sequence/AUTO_INCREMENT values — gaps in IDs are normal and not a bug

chapters.title: ACID, One Letter at a Time
points: Atomicity: all statements commit or none do; implemented by undo logs / rollback segments
Consistency: the transaction takes the DB from one valid state to another, enforcing constraints, FKs, triggers — largely the application's and schema's job, not magic
Isolation: concurrent transactions must not see each other's partial work; this is the only letter with a tunable dial
Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash; implemented by write-ahead logging plus fsync
Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) rule: the log record must hit stable storage before the data page does
Postgres synchronous_commit and MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1|2|0 — the exact knobs that trade durability for throughput
Example: a crash right after COMMIT returns — recovery replays the redo log and reapplies the change
Comparison: ACID vs BASE (eventually consistent stores) and why distributed systems relax the letters
Common misconception: 'Consistency' in ACID is not the 'C' in CAP theorem — different meanings entirely

chapters.title: The Four Read Anomalies
points: Dirty read: T1 reads a row that T2 wrote but has not committed; if T2 rolls back, T1 acted on data that never existed
Non-repeatable read: T1 reads a row twice and gets different values because T2 committed an UPDATE in between
Phantom read: T1 runs the same range query twice and the second run returns new rows because T2 committed an INSERT matching the predicate
Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value, and the second write silently overwrites the first
Write skew: two transactions each read a set, verify an invariant, and write disjoint rows — each is fine alone, together they break the invariant (on-call doctor example: both doctors go off shift)
Read skew: T1 reads row X, T2 updates X and Y and commits, T1 reads Y — the pair is mutually inconsistent
Concrete dirty-read walkthrough with two numbered timelines and account balances
The anomaly hierarchy: each stronger isolation level removes anomalies from the top of this list
Anomalies are about interleaving, not speed — a slow query is not more likely to be wrong, but it is exposed for longer

chapters.title: The Four Standard Isolation Levels
points: READ UNCOMMITTED: dirty reads allowed; almost never useful; in Postgres it silently behaves as READ COMMITTED
READ COMMITTED: each statement sees only committed data as of statement start; default in Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server
REPEATABLE READ: all reads see a snapshot as of transaction start; default in MySQL InnoDB
SERIALIZABLE: result must be equivalent to some serial ordering of the transactions
The ANSI anomaly table: level × {dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom} with allowed/prevented per cell
Syntax: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; and the session-scoped SET SESSION TRANSACTION ... variant
How to check the current level: SHOW transaction_isolation (Postgres), SELECT @@transaction_isolation (MySQL), DBCC USEROPTIONS (SQL Server)
The ANSI standard defines levels by which anomalies they forbid — engines are free to be stricter, which is why defaults differ
Postgres REPEATABLE READ blocks phantoms (snapshot isolation) even though ANSI permits them
MySQL REPEATABLE READ blocks phantoms for plain SELECT via MVCC but not for locking reads without gap locks

chapters.title: MVCC: How Snapshots Are Built
points: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: writers create new row versions instead of overwriting, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers
Postgres row headers: xmin (creating transaction) and xmax (deleting transaction) decide visibility
The snapshot: a transaction records the set of in-progress XIDs; a row version is visible if xmin committed before the snapshot and xmax did not
MySQL InnoDB undo log and roll pointers: old versions are reconstructed by walking the undo chain backward
READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot for the whole transaction
Dead tuples and bloat: VACUUM in Postgres, purge threads in InnoDB reclaim versions no snapshot can still see
A long-running transaction pins the oldest snapshot and blocks cleanup — the classic cause of table bloat and 'idle in transaction' pages
Example: idle-in-transaction session held open for hours grows a hot table's disk usage several times over
Comparison: MVCC (Postgres, InnoDB, Oracle) vs pure two-phase locking (older SQL Server default) for read behavior
SQL Server READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT and SNAPSHOT isolation use tempdb version store rather than in-page versions

chapters.title: Locks: Shared, Exclusive, and Everything Between
points: Lock modes: shared (S) for reads, exclusive (X) for writes, and the compatibility matrix between them
Intent locks (IS, IX, SIX): announce at the table level what you plan to do at row level, so table-level requests need not scan every row
Granularity ladder: row lock, page lock, table lock, and lock escalation when a statement touches too many rows
Two-Phase Locking (2PL): a growing phase acquires locks, a shrinking phase releases them; strict 2PL holds all locks to COMMIT
Record locks, gap locks, and next-key locks in InnoDB — how gap locks stop phantoms by locking the space between index entries
Predicate locks / SIREAD locks in Postgres Serializable Snapshot Isolation track read dependencies instead of blocking
Explicit locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE, and LOCK TABLE
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and NOWAIT for queue-style workloads that must not pile up behind one row
Locks are held to end of transaction, not end of statement — a long transaction after a write starves everyone on that row
Inspecting locks: pg_locks joined to pg_stat_activity, MySQL performance_schema.data_locks, sys.dm_tran_locks

chapters.title: Deadlocks: Detection, Cause, and Cure
points: Definition: two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs, forming a cycle in the wait-for graph
The minimal example: T1 updates row A then row B; T2 updates row B then row A
Detection: the engine builds a wait-for graph, finds the cycle, and kills a victim — Postgres after deadlock_timeout (default 1s), InnoDB near-instantly
The victim is usually the transaction with the least work done / fewest undo records; the client sees SQLSTATE 40P01 or MySQL error 1213
Prevention by ordering: always touch rows in a consistent order (for example, sort account IDs before updating)
Prevention by shrinking: keep transactions short, do not hold locks across network calls or user think-time
Timeouts as a blunt tool: innodb_lock_wait_timeout, lock_timeout, statement_timeout — these stop lock waits, not true deadlocks
Deadlocks caused by index choice: a table scan takes more locks than an index seek, widening the window
Reading the evidence: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS 'LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK', Postgres log deadlock detail, SQL Server deadlock graph
Mistake: treating deadlock as a fatal bug — deadlocks are expected under concurrency, so retry the whole transaction with backoff
Deadlock vs lock wait vs livelock: distinguishing them before choosing a fix

chapters.title: Serializable in Practice
points: Two implementations: locking serializability (strict 2PL, real blocking) vs Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI, optimistic)
Postgres SSI tracks rw-dependencies and aborts a transaction with 'could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies' (SQLSTATE 40001)
SSI means any transaction can fail at COMMIT — your application MUST have a retry loop, not a try/catch that logs
Retry pattern: catch 40001/40P01, roll back, sleep with jitter, replay the whole transaction from the beginning, cap at N attempts
Retries must replay reads too — reusing values read in the failed attempt reintroduces the anomaly you paid for
MySQL SERIALIZABLE degrades to implicitly adding LOCK IN SHARE MODE to every SELECT — pessimistic, and much slower
SQL Server SNAPSHOT vs SERIALIZABLE: SNAPSHOT is optimistic with update conflicts; SERIALIZABLE takes range locks
Cost: SSI adds predicate-lock bookkeeping and false-positive aborts; abort rate rises sharply with contention and long transactions
When SERIALIZABLE earns its keep: financial invariants, booking systems, anything with a write-skew shaped rule
Cheaper alternatives that handle specific cases: SELECT FOR UPDATE, a unique constraint, or a single atomic UPDATE ... WHERE

chapters.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Concurrency
points: Pessimistic: lock first, assume conflict — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE then UPDATE then COMMIT
Optimistic: read freely, verify at write time with a version column — UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, then check the affected row count
The lost-update problem solved both ways, side by side, with the same two-user scenario
Compare-and-set as a single statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100 avoids the read-modify-write race entirely
Trade-off table: contention level, retry cost, lock-hold duration, deadlock risk, and reader impact for each approach
Rule of thumb: pessimistic wins under high contention on few rows; optimistic wins when conflicts are rare
ORM traps: Hibernate @Version, Django select_for_update(), Rails with_lock — and what they actually emit
Advisory locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock, GET_LOCK) for application-level mutual exclusion outside the row model
Idempotency keys and unique constraints as the concurrency control of last resort for retried API calls

chapters.title: Engine Differences and Performance Trade-offs
points: Default level per engine: Postgres READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, SQL Server READ COMMITTED (locking), Oracle READ COMMITTED
MySQL REPEATABLE READ quirk: locking reads (FOR UPDATE) see the latest committed row, not the snapshot — a documented source of surprise
Postgres READ COMMITTED UPDATE re-evaluation: a blocked UPDATE re-checks its WHERE clause against the new row version after the blocker commits
SQL Server's READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON turns the default into a non-blocking versioned read — usually the single highest-value setting change
Cost model: stronger isolation buys correctness with lock waits, version-store I/O, and abort-and-retry work
Long transactions are the universal enemy: bloat, replication lag, blocked DDL, lock pileups, and larger deadlock windows
Connection-pool interaction: a pooled connection left mid-transaction leaks isolation settings and locks to the next borrower
Read replicas offer snapshot reads at the price of replication lag — not a substitute for isolation
Measuring: pg_stat_activity wait_event, MySQL innodb_row_lock_time_avg, SQL Server blocking chains via sys.dm_exec_requests
Benchmarking rule: measure abort/retry rate alongside throughput, since retries hide as latency, not errors

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and How They Bite
points: Doing read-modify-write in application code without a version check or a lock — the number-one lost-update source
Holding a transaction open across an HTTP call, message publish, or user prompt
Assuming SELECT ... then INSERT is safe against duplicates — only a unique constraint truly prevents them
Catching the serialization-failure exception and swallowing it instead of retrying the transaction
Raising isolation to SERIALIZABLE as a shotgun fix, then losing throughput to aborts nobody retries
Running a long analytics query inside a write transaction and pinning the oldest snapshot
Mixing DDL into a transaction on MySQL and unknowingly committing early
Forgetting that ROLLBACK does not undo side effects outside the DB: sent emails, queued jobs, file writes
Trusting an ORM's default transaction boundaries without reading the emitted SQL
Retrying a non-idempotent transaction without an idempotency key, causing a double charge
Setting a lock timeout but no statement timeout, so a runaway query still blocks the queue

chapters.title: Transactions Cheat Sheet
points: ACID in one line each: Atomicity = all or nothing, Consistency = valid states, Isolation = as if alone, Durability = survives crash
Anomaly matrix: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty/non-repeatable/phantom; READ COMMITTED allows non-repeatable/phantom; REPEATABLE READ allows phantom (per ANSI); SERIALIZABLE allows none
Defaults: Postgres RC, MySQL RR, SQL Server RC (locking), Oracle RC
Syntax block: BEGIN; SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ...; SAVEPOINT sp; ROLLBACK TO sp; COMMIT;
Locking reads: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE | FOR SHARE | FOR UPDATE NOWAIT | FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Error codes to retry: 40001 serialization failure, 40P01 deadlock detected, MySQL 1213 deadlock, 1205 lock wait timeout
Diagnostic commands: pg_locks + pg_stat_activity, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, sys.dm_tran_locks, EXPLAIN to shrink the lock footprint
Timeout knobs: lock_timeout, statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, innodb_lock_wait_timeout
Decision rule: default RC + explicit FOR UPDATE or CAS for hot rows; escalate to SERIALIZABLE only for invariants across rows, with retries
Five habits: keep transactions short, order writes consistently, retry on 40001/40P01, never wait on humans or networks inside a transaction, enforce invariants with constraints where you can
